Hull approaching an anchorage in the lower end of Iliuliuk Bay, in the Aleutian Islands, North Pacific, 27 Apr 1937

USS Hull (DD 350) was a Farragut-class destroyer that had a remarkable but ultimately tragic career in the United States Navy.

Hull was laid down on March 7, 1933, at the New York Navy Yard in Brooklyn, launched on January 31, 1934, and commissioned on January 11, 1935. She was named after Commodore Isaac Hull, the famed commander of USS Constitution. The Farragut class represented the first new destroyers built for the U.S. Navy since the end of World War I, and they were significantly larger and more capable than the older flush-deck destroyers they were designed to supplement.

She displaced about 1,395 tons standard (over 2,000 tons fully loaded), measured 341 feet 3 inches in length, and had a beam of 34 feet 3 inches. Her geared steam turbines produced 42,800 shaft horsepower, giving her a top speed of around 36.5 knots. Her armament originally included five 5-inch/38 caliber dual-purpose guns, four .50 caliber machine guns, and eight 21-inch torpedo tubes. During the war, her anti-aircraft armament was significantly upgraded with 20mm and 40mm guns.

Hull spent her early years operating in the Pacific, conducting training exercises, fleet maneuvers, and goodwill cruises. She was based at San Diego and later Pearl Harbor as tensions with Japan rose throughout the late 1930s.

On December 7, 1941, Hull was moored at Pearl Harbor when the Japanese attack began. She got underway during the attack and contributed anti-aircraft fire against the attacking aircraft, though she was not significantly damaged. She immediately joined patrol and escort operations following the attack.

Hull had an extensive Pacific war record. She participated in the early carrier raids in 1942, escorted convoys, and supported the Aleutian Islands campaign in 1942 and 1943, including operations against Kiska and Attu. She then moved south to participate in the Central Pacific drive, supporting operations in the Gilbert and Marshall Islands in late 1943 and early 1944.

She participated in the Marianas campaign in mid-1944, including the invasions of Saipan, Tinian, and Guam, and the Battle of the Philippine Sea. She then supported operations in the Western Carolines and the invasion of the Philippines, screening fast carrier task forces during strikes against Japanese positions.

Hull's end came on December 18, 1944, during one of the worst weather disasters in U.S. Navy history. Task Force 38, under Admiral William "Bull" Halsey, was operating east of the Philippines, conducting air strikes in support of the Mindoro landings and refueling at sea. The fleet was caught by a powerful typhoon, later known as Typhoon Cobra or Halsey's Typhoon.

Hull, low on fuel and therefore riding higher and less stable than she would have been with full bunkers, was caught in the worst of the storm. Winds reached over 100 knots with gusts higher, and seas were estimated at 70 feet or more. Her commanding officer, Lieutenant Commander James A. Marks, struggled to keep her into the wind, but eventually Hull was pinned on her beam ends by sustained hurricane-force winds. Water poured down her stacks and through ventilators, and she could not right herself. She rolled over and sank.

Of her crew of approximately 264 men, only 62 survived. Survivors clung to floating debris and life rafts for up to 50 hours before being rescued, primarily by the destroyer escort USS Tabberer (DE 418), whose captain, Lieutenant Commander Henry Lee Plage, conducted heroic rescue operations against orders to rejoin the fleet, saving 55 men from Hull and other lost ships.

Two other destroyers, USS Spence (DD 512) and USS Monaghan (DD 354), were also lost in the typhoon. In total, 790 sailors died, three ships were lost, and approximately 100 aircraft were destroyed or damaged across the fleet.

A naval court of inquiry investigated the disaster. While the court found that primary responsibility lay with Admiral Halsey for keeping his fleet in the path of the storm, it stopped short of recommending disciplinary action, citing the difficult operational circumstances. The disaster led to major reforms in Navy weather forecasting, the establishment of better typhoon warning systems in the Pacific, and revised guidance on fleet maneuvering in severe weather. Ship stability standards were also reviewed, particularly regarding the importance of maintaining adequate ballast in light displacement conditions.

Hull received 10 battle stars for her World War II service. The story of her loss, along with the broader Typhoon Cobra disaster, was famously recounted in Herman Wouk's novel "The Caine Mutiny," which was inspired in part by these events, as Wouk had served on destroyer-minesweepers in the Pacific during the war.
